title: Galvanic Cells
lead: Copper placed in a solution of silver ions gives its electrons to them directly. A galvanic cell separates such a pair of reactants into two half-cells, sends the electrons through an external circuit and keeps the charge balanced through a salt bridge, and a cell schematic writes the whole arrangement in one line.
objectives: Describe the function of a galvanic cell and its components
Use cell notation to symbolize the composition and construction of galvanic cells
summary_html: Galvanic cells are devices in which a spontaneous redox reaction occurs indirectly, with the oxidant and reductant redox couples contained in separate half-cells. Electrons are transferred from the reductant (in the anode half-cell) to the oxidant (in the cathode half-cell) through an external circuit, and inert solution phase ions are transferred between half-cells, through a salt bridge, to maintain charge neutrality. The construction and composition of a galvanic cell may be succinctly represented using chemical formulas and others symbols in the form of a cell schematic (cell notation).
notes: Nothing of the section is left out. The overall equation’s Cu^{2}{}^{+} and the misplaced parenthesis in the key of exercise fs-idm154595184 (d), “(aq), Cu²⁺”, are kept as printed.

exercises.prompt:
Omitting solute concentrations and spectator ion identities, write the schematic for a galvanic cell whose net cell reaction is shown below.
${\text{Sn}}^{4+}(aq)+\text{Zn}(s)\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{Sn}}^{2+}(aq)+{\text{Zn}}^{2+}(aq)$

Write cell schematics for the following cell reactions, using platinum as an inert electrode as needed.
(a) $\text{Mg}(s)+{\text{Ni}}^{2+}(aq)\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{Mg}}^{2+}(aq)+\text{Ni}(s)$
(b) $2{\text{Ag}}^{\text{+}}(aq)+\text{Cu}(s)\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{Cu}}^{2+}(aq)+\text{2Ag}(s)$
(c) $\text{Mn}(s)+{\text{Sn(NO}}_{3}{)}_{2}(aq)\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{Mn(NO}}_{3}{)}_{2}(aq)+\text{Sn}(s)$
(d) $3{\text{CuNO}}_{3}(aq)+{\text{Au(NO}}_{3}{)}_{3}(aq)\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{3Cu(NO}}_{3}{)}_{2}(aq)+\text{Au}(s)$

Write a balanced equation for the cell reaction of each cell in the exercise that gives these two schematics, which represent galvanic cells as written:
(a) $\text{Mg}(s)\,|\,{\text{Mg}}^{2+}(aq)\,\|\,{\text{Cu}}^{2+}(aq)\,|\,\text{Cu}(s)$
(b) $\text{Ni}(s)\,|\,\;{\text{Ni}}^{2+}(aq)\,\|\,{\text{Ag}}^{\text{+}}(aq)\,|\,\;\text{Ag}(s)$

Identify the oxidant and reductant in each reaction of the exercise that asks for these reactions to be balanced:
(a) $\text{Al}(s)+{\text{Zr}}^{4+}(aq)\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{Al}}^{3+}(aq)+\text{Zr}(s)$
(b) ${\text{Ag}}^{\text{+}}(aq)+\text{NO}(g)\;\longrightarrow \;\text{Ag}(s)+{\text{NO}}_{3}{}^{\text{−}}(aq)\hspace{5em}(\text{acidic solution})$
(c) ${\text{SiO}}_{3}{}^{2−}(aq)+\text{Mg}(s)\;\longrightarrow \;\text{Si}(s)+\text{Mg}{(\text{OH})}_{2}(s)\hspace{5em}\text{(basic solution)}$
(d) ${\text{ClO}}_{3}{}^{\text{−}}(aq)+{\text{MnO}}_{2}(s)\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{Cl}}^{\text{−}}(aq)+{\text{MnO}}_{4}{}^{\text{−}}(aq)\hspace{5em}\text{(basic solution)}$

answer.solution: Species oxidized = reducing agent: (a) Al(s); (b) NO(g); (c) Mg(s); and (d) MnO2(s); Species reduced = oxidizing agent: (a) Zr4+(aq); (b) Ag+(aq); (c) ${\text{SiO}}_{3}{}^{2−}(aq)$; and (d) ${\text{ClO}}_{3}{}^{\text{−}}(aq)$

exercises.prompt: Why is a salt bridge necessary in galvanic cells like the one in Figure 17.3?

answer.solution: Without the salt bridge, the circuit would be open (or broken) and no current could flow. With a salt bridge, each half-cell remains electrically neutral and current can flow through the circuit.

exercises.prompt: An active (metal) electrode was found to gain mass as the oxidation-reduction reaction was allowed to proceed. Was the electrode an anode or a cathode? Explain.

answer.solution: Suggested approach: an active electrode is made of a member of its half-cell’s redox couple. Ask which half-reaction turns metal ions in the solution into atoms of the metal on the electrode’s surface, oxidation or reduction, and then at which electrode that half-reaction occurs, as for the silver foil of Figure 17.3.

exercises.prompt: An active (metal) electrode was found to lose mass as the oxidation-reduction reaction was allowed to proceed. Was the electrode an anode or a cathode? Explain.

answer.solution: Active electrodes participate in the oxidation-reduction reaction. Since metals form cations, the electrode would lose mass if metal atoms in the electrode were to oxidize and go into solution. Oxidation occurs at the anode.

exercises.prompt: The masses of three electrodes (A, B, and C), each from three different galvanic cells, were measured before and after the cells were allowed to pass current for a while. The mass of electrode A increased, that of electrode B was unchanged, and that of electrode C decreased. Identify each electrode as active or inert, and note (if possible) whether it functioned as anode or cathode.

answer.solution: Suggested approach: an inert electrode is neither oxidized nor reduced, so its mass does not change, while an active electrode’s mass changes as its metal dissolves or deposits. Decide first which electrodes are active, then, for each active one, whether metal left it as cations (oxidation) or was deposited on it (reduction), and name the electrode where that occurs. For the unchanged electrode, ask whether its mass alone can tell which half-reaction took place at it.
